title: How to grid your fabric for cross-stitch
subtitle: Marking a 10x10 basting grid to keep counting accurate on large pieces
excerpt: Gridding a piece of Aida before stitching means marking a grid of basting threads every ten squares in both directions, matching the 10-by-10 grid that most charts print. A counted cross-stitch with a gridded fabric is faster to navigate and much less likely to accumulate counting errors over a long project.
sourceNotes: The 10x10 basting grid is a widely documented accuracy technique in counted cross-stitch, standard practice for complex or large-format pieces.

glossaryTerms.definition: The practice of marking a 10-by-10-square basting grid on cross-stitch fabric before stitching, matching the chart's 10x10 grid. The grid helps count large pieces accurately and is removed when the stitching is finished.

A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

A long, loose running stitch in a contrasting thread, used to mark a temporary guide on fabric. In cross-stitch, basting creates the 10-by-10 counting grid; the threads are pulled out when stitching is done.

content.text: means sewing a light grid of

threads every ten squares in both directions. The grid lines up with the 10-by-10 counting blocks most printed charts show as a darker grid line, so you always know at a glance exactly where you are on the chart without recounting from the edge.

Gridding adds setup time at the start of a project. For pieces with fewer than about 100 stitches in any direction the benefit is small. For a sampler, a landscape, or any design larger than a 10-cm square, the grid quickly pays back the time by eliminating miscounts. A wrong count on an ungridded large piece may not become visible for dozens of stitches.
Thread a needle with a single contrasting strand of light-coloured
. Do not knot it. White or pale grey is a useful choice; it shows against both dark and light Aida without staining.
Find the centre of the fabric. Work outward from the centre in rows of ten squares, placing a basting stitch over every tenth vertical column of holes from top to bottom of the piece.

Each basting stitch runs along a vertical thread of the Aida weave: down one hole, up the next, down the next, in a running stitch along the line. The thread lies in the channel between the woven blocks, which means it will not be stitched over and will come out cleanly at the end.
Repeat for horizontal rows, basting a line every ten holes across the fabric width.
Remove the grid lines when the piece is finished by pulling the basting threads out from the edge, going in the same direction they were placed.

items.symptom: The basting thread leaves a faint colour trace after removal
items.cause: A dark or bright coloured floss was used for the basting.
items.fix: Always use white, pale grey, or ivory basting thread. On dark Aida, use a pale colour that is clearly visible without being saturated.

items.symptom: The grid lines do not align with the chart's 10x10 grid
items.cause: The centre of the fabric was not used as the starting point for counting.
items.fix: Start from the fabric centre and count outward in each direction. The chart centre and fabric centre should correspond; grid lines placed from this shared centre will match the chart grid.

content.text: A gridded fabric is the standard setup for a complex sampler. Once the grid is in place, work the piece section by section across each 10-by-10 block, matching each block to the corresponding square on the chart before placing the first stitch.
